newsitem.title: USA: PSE&G urges adoption of EPA NOx standards.
newsitem.headline: PSE&G urges adoption of EPA NOx standards.

text.p: Public Service Electric & Gas Co President Lawrence R. Codey Tuesday urged adoption of Environmental Protection Agency's nitrogen oxide emission standards as part of a four-point strategy designed to advance achievement of national clean air goals as the electric industry makes the transition to competition.

In a speech before the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, Codey asserted "the ability to pollute the environment and degrade public health and safety should not become a competitive advantage. Pollution should not enhance the bottom line."

Codey called on lawmakers and regulators at the federal level and in PSE&G's home state of New Jersey to implement environmental standards necessary to ensure that electric industry restructuring doesn't create a system favoring the dirtiest and, therefore, cheapest sources of generation.
The four-point strategy outlined by Codey includes:

-- Implementation of EPA'S recommended cap of 650,000- to-one million tons of NOx emissions by electric plants in the nation's 37 eastern-most states. NOx is a primary contributor to creation of ground-level ozone, a persistent, serious public health problem afflicting many areas in this region.
-- Achieving emissions reductions necessary to meet the cap through implementation of uniform power-plant NOx emissions standards throughout the 37-state region.
-- Establishing an NOx emissions trading system that will make maximum use of the most cost-effective emissions reductions technology and techniques.
-- Implementation of more stringent national ambient air quality standards for ozone and fine particulate matter (soot) now being proposed by the EPA.

In addition to these regional strategies, he noted, PSE&G also has called on New Jersey regulators to impose stringent air quality requirements for all in-state and out-of-state power suppliers seeking to participate in the state's competitive electricity market.
In comments filed previously with state regulators, the Public Service Enterprise Group Inc subsidiary recommended that New Jersey:
-- Establish and enforce emissions standards for all marketers doing business in the state.
-- Expand New Jersey's emissions trading program to cover all components of the emissions standards.
-- Require that any energy provider selling power in the state whose generation facilities do not meet the established emissions standards purchase the appropriate amount of emissions credits.

The atmospheric transport of hundreds of thousands of tons of NOx and other pollutants from electric generating plants in the Midwest, South and Ohio Valley into the Northeast's airshed has been most recently documented, Codey said, by a detailed study issued by the Northeast States for Coordinated Air Use Management, a consortium of state environmental commissioners.

The effect of increased pollution from wholesale competition alone, he said, "will offset and overwhelm the billions of dollars we've spent to reduce ozone in the Northeast on power plant cleanups, use of reformulated gasoline, enhanced motor vehicle inspection and maintenance programs, and other controls and restrictions affecting large and small businesses."
